issues.legal_issue: A dominant owner may not alter the mode or place of enjoying a drainage easement so as to increase the burden on the servient property.
material_facts: The owners had previously discharged water through three outlets, and an earlier decree protected that arrangement.
After raising and extending their structure, the dominant owners blocked the original outlets and opened nine new outlets directed towards the neighbouring properties.
The increased discharge from the new outlets damaged the neighbouring properties.
issues.conclusion: The new outlets imposed an additional burden on the servient properties, so the statutory right to alter the mode or place of enjoying an easement did not protect their use; the injunction against using them was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 permits a dominant owner to alter the mode and place of enjoying an easement only if no additional burden is imposed on the servient heritage. Harvey v. Walters, [1872-73] L.R. 8 C.P. 162, was distinguished because the alteration there did not increase the burden.

predicates.drainage_easement_case: A dispute concerns a dominant owner's use of a drainage easement over another person's property.
predicates.outlet_count_increased: The dominant owner replaced the earlier drainage arrangement with a greater number of outlets.
predicates.increased_discharge_damaged_servient_pro: The new arrangement directed increased water discharge onto the servient property and caused damage there.

issues.definition: When a drainage-easement dispute involves more outlets and increased discharge that damages the servient property, use of the new outlets may be enjoined.

issues.legal_issue: A party need not be permitted to raise for the first time in a special-leave appeal an easement contention that would require further evidence when its conduct has damaged the other party's property.
material_facts: The owners argued at the Supreme Court stage that three of the new outlets merely changed the mode or place of enjoying the earlier easement.
They had not raised that contention below, and deciding it would have required a remand for further evidence.
Their conduct in opening nine outlets in place of three had damaged the neighbouring properties.
issues.conclusion: The new contention could not be raised at that stage, and the Court declined to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction to assist the appellants.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court may decline to entertain a contention raised for the first time at that stage, particularly where it was not considered by the courts below, would require further evidence and remand, and arises from conduct that caused damage.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and contention_not_raised_below and deciding_contention_requires_remand and party_conduct_caused_property_damage

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.contention_not_raised_below: The party did not raise the contention in the courts below.
predicates.deciding_contention_requires_remand: Resolving the contention would require further evidence and a remand.
predicates.party_conduct_caused_property_damage: The party's conduct caused damage to another person's property.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, a contention not raised below need not be considered when deciding it requires a remand and the party's conduct caused property damage.

issues.legal_issue: A property owner cannot prevent a neighbour from opening windows in the absence of a pleaded and proved customary right of privacy, but may block those windows without the neighbour damaging the blocking walls.
material_facts: The owners opened new windows facing the neighbouring houses.
The neighbours raised their walls to block the windows.
No customary right of privacy had been pleaded or proved.
The owners claimed a right to break the walls obstructing the view from their windows.
issues.conclusion: The owners could not be restrained from opening the new windows, but the neighbours could block them, and the owners could not break or damage the blocking walls.
issues.legal_principle: A person may use their property in any manner permitted by law; without a pleaded and proved customary right of privacy, neighbours cannot obtain an injunction preventing new windows from being opened. The neighbours remain entitled to block the windows, and the window owners may not damage the walls to remove that obstruction.

predicates.new_windows_face_neighbouring_property: A property owner opens new windows facing a neighbour's property.
predicates.no_customary_privacy_right_proved: The neighbour has not pleaded and proved a customary right of privacy.
predicates.neighbour_erects_blocking_walls: The neighbour raises or erects walls to block the new windows.

issues.definition: When new windows face neighbouring property, no customary privacy right is proved, and the neighbour erects blocking walls, the windows cannot be enjoined and the walls must not be damaged.
